items.title: 68429_Walter P. Thomas oral history interview
items.q: [INTERVIEWER] He surrounded himself with Don Byas and Budd Johnson.

ctx.x: It's the most... For a Jazz solo, it's the most accurate Jazz solo ever written. Because the miraculous thing he did, it changes keys three times. And he modulated into each change of key. And he almost had to have planned that solo before. Because he started out... [SINGS]...started out with the melody. That's how he started it, very melodic. And one thing, when he recorded "Body and Soul," ain't nobody said nothin' about Coleman since. Now, when Bebop come along, he played Bebop just as good as any of the Bebop…
He surrounded himself with Don Byas and Budd Johnson.

He just played it as good as any of them. He changed his style, as I know of, three times; maybe four, because I don't know what he did before he changed to tenor. But when I checked with his mother and she said he played cello, I said to myself that's why he had that feeling for that sound. See, because the tenor is closer to cello than anything else. The only thing that's closer to cello is the baritone. But he was a genius.
